title: Prohibiciones, deudas y proteínas: la economía de la IA se reordena
script:
Bienvenidos a Radio IA, hoy es 25 de noviembre de 2026. Empezamos con una jornada en la que la inteligencia artificial toca tres frentes a la vez: la protección de los niños, la batalla por el comercio electrónico y el avance silencioso de los modelos que diseñan biología. Hoy hay varias historias que muestran cómo la regulación, la deuda y la ciencia están empujando a la industria en direcciones opuestas.

La primera historia nos lleva a Nueva York. La gobernadora Kathy Hochul firmó una ley que prohíbe durante cinco años la fabricación y venta de juguetes impulsados por chatbots de inteligencia artificial, incluidos peluches parlantes, muñecas y robots que usan internet para conversar con niños. Según The Guardian, la gobernadora dijo que los padres no deberían tener que preocuparse de que chatbots peligrosos disfrazados de juguete expongan a sus hijos a conversaciones inapropiadas, manipulen sus sentimientos o pongan en riesgo su privacidad. La fiscal general Letitia James añadió que los chatbots en juguetes infantiles exponen a los jóvenes a contenido inapropiado y ponen en riesgo su salud mental, y que su oficina no dudará en aplicar esta ley. El texto menciona un estudio de NBC News que encontró que un juguete llamado Pixie Paw, comercializado para niños desde los tres años, compartió detalles sobre pelotones de fusilamiento y masacres, y que el Pixie Paw Smart Interactive Plush Cat explicó violación en grupo. También cita un informe de consumidores que probó juguetes con chatbot y encontró que hablaban en profundidad sobre temas sexualmente explícitos, decían a los niños dónde probablemente encontrar cerillas en casa y actuaban molestos cuando un niño tenía que irse. La gobernadora señaló que algunos juguetes tenían pocos o ningún control parental, que los límites de seguridad se debilitaban cuanto más larga era la conversación y que algunos podían grabar la voz o escanear la cara del niño. Mi lectura es que esta prohibición convierte a Nueva York en un laboratorio regulatorio que puede encarecer el cumplimiento para los fabricantes de juguetes conectados y acelerar la salida de estos productos del canal minorista tradicional, justo cuando las marcas buscaban diferenciarse con compañeros artificiales para niños.

Seguimos con el comercio electrónico. Según The Verge, Amazon ha mantenido conversaciones para permitir que el agente de inteligencia artificial Muse, de Meta, compre en su mercado en línea. Las discusiones, según un informe de Fortune, giran en torno a los tipos de productos que el agente recomienda y el posible impacto en los ingresos publicitarios del gigante del comercio. Amazon está preocupada por perder ingresos publicitarios si permite a Muse en su sitio, porque depende de que humanos reales vean anuncios en su mercado. También le preocupa la calidad de los resultados de búsqueda de productos que Muse presentará a los usuarios y si el agente afectará su relación con los clientes. The Verge recuerda que minoristas como Walmart, Best Buy, Gap y Sephora han abierto sus puertas digitales a agentes como Muse, pero Amazon ha sido más reticente. Amazon también bloqueó al agente de Perplexity y en su lugar ha impulsado su propio asistente Alexa for Shopping. Mi lectura es que esta negociación es una señal de que Amazon está tratando de evitar ceder el escaparate a intermediarios de Meta sin cobrar un peaje equivalente al que hoy obtiene por publicidad; si cierra un acuerdo, el precio de aparecer recomendado por un agente externo podría convertirse en una nueva línea de ingresos.

Pasamos a una advertencia desde Sudáfrica. Según Bloomberg Technology, el banco central de Sudáfrica considera que el auge de deuda de los hiperescaladores representa un riesgo. El endeudamiento soberano está compitiendo con el aumento de emisiones de las empresas de inteligencia artificial, y los inversores locales están colocando una mayor proporción de fondos en acciones de hiperescaladores, lo que podría elevar tanto los rendimientos como los riesgos. Esa es la información disponible, y no hay más detalles en esta fuente. Mi lectura es que este aviso refleja un temor creciente entre bancos centrales de mercados emergentes: si el capital local fluye hacia acciones tecnológicas estadounidenses y deuda corporativa ligada a centros de datos, los gobiernos pueden tener que pagar más por financiarse exactamente cuando más necesitan inversión doméstica estable.

Ahora nos vamos a Australia, donde las universidades están cambiando la forma de evaluar. Según The Guardian, la Universidad de Sídney ha exigido que todos los estudiantes de su programa de honores defiendan oralmente sus argumentos ante profesores, y es la primera gran institución australiana en imponerlo en todos los programas de honores. El artículo cuenta que Aidan Elwig Pollock, estudiante de historia, no esperaba que su tesis de 20,000 palabras viniera acompañada de un componente hablado, y lo consideró insultante. En su caso, la conversación fue una prueba de aprobar o suspender sin valor en la nota final, pero no obtendrá el título si no la supera. Una estudiante de ingeniería, identificada con seudónimo, contó que su entrevista con profesores duró una hora en una sala con cinco compañeros, con gente entrando y saliendo, y que representó el 50% de su calificación mientras su tesis de 20,000 palabras valió solo el 20%. El artículo dice que exámenes han pasado de computadoras a papel o entrevistas en los cuatro años desde el lanzamiento de ChatGPT, y que otras universidades como Melbourne, Monash y la Universidad Católica Australiana están incorporando evaluaciones orales. Mi lectura es que este movimiento tiene un coste económico directo: las entrevistas aumentan la carga de trabajo de los profesores sin que, según el artículo, se hayan contratado casuales para ayudar, y al mismo tiempo redistribuyen el peso de las notas desde el trabajo escrito hacia el desempeño verbal, lo que puede alterar qué estudiantes acceden a acreditaciones profesionales.

Y cerramos con ciencia. Según OpenAI News, la familia de modelos GPT-6 demuestra capacidades intrínsecas para diseñar proteínas. Los modelos pueden diseñar nuevas formas de proteínas y las secuencias de sus bloques químicos usando solo razonamiento y código, sin llamar a modelos biológicos especializados. En pruebas de laboratorio con Onava, proteínas basadas en diseños de GPT-6.2 mostraron evidencia de unión, o acoplamiento, en cinco objetivos. El texto detalla que probaron 322 miniproteínas contra 5 objetivos en el laboratorio y que 35 de ellas dieron positivo en unión a su objetivo previsto, lo que equivale al 10,9%. También vieron unión en 75 de 88 diseños para MDM2, lo que supone un 85%, en 26 de 42 para VEGF-A, un 62%, y en 8 de 59 para PD-1, un 14%. Los modelos se apoyaron en matemáticas, física, química y código, y aunque la predicción completa de estructura proteica seguía siendo una debilidad clara, su desempeño fue comparable o mejor que el de modelos especializados en la mayoría de tareas. Mi lectura es que esto cambia el cálculo económico del descubrimiento de fármacos: si un modelo generalista puede sustituir parte del trabajo de varios modelos especializados y aceptar nuevas instrucciones sin reentrenamiento, los laboratorios podrían gastar menos en licencias y personal experto, y más en validación experimental temprana como la que ya se hizo con Onava.

Qué mirar mañana: habrá que seguir si algún gran minorista reacciona a la prohibición de Nueva York retirando voluntariamente juguetes con chatbot de sus catálogos en otros estados, y si Amazon o Meta confirman públicamente sus conversaciones sobre el agente Muse. También conviene observar si algún otro banco central, sobre todo en economías emergentes, se suma al aviso sudafricano sobre la deuda de los hiperescaladores, y si OpenAI publica datos adicionales de laboratorio sobre los diseños de proteínas de GPT-6. Terminamos aquí por hoy. Gracias por escuchar Radio IA, nos encontramos mañana con más historias sobre inteligencia artificial y su impacto económico.

stories.title: New York bans AI toys, including those using internet to talk to children
stories.summary:
The state attorney general says she would ‘not hesitate to enforce’ the five-year ban signed by governor Kathy Hochul

The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, signed legislation on Wednesday that places a five year ban on the manufacture and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children.

The recently re-elected governor, who has also placed a one-year moratorium AI datacenter construction in the state, said that parents shopping for children’s toys “should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk”.

Continue reading...
stories.body:
The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, signed legislation on Wednesday that places a five year ban on the manufacture and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children.
The recently re-elected governor, who has also placed a one-year moratorium AI datacenter construction in the state, said that parents shopping for children’s toys “should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk”.
Hochul said the measure was “deeply personal” and that, as a mother and grandmother, “it’s my job to put New York families first.”
A study by NBC News found that the Pixie Paw, a toy marketed to children as young as three, had shared details about firing squads and massacres. It also found that Pixie Paw Smart Interactive Plush Cat explained gang rape.
The New York attorney general, Letitia James, added that AI chatbots in children’s toys “are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk”.
James said that her office would “not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm. We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”
In a press release, the officials pointed to “Trouble in Toyland”, a consumer watchdog report from the US Public Interest Research Group Education Fund (PIRG), that tested AI chatbot-enabled toys marketed to children as young as three that “talked in depth about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave.”
The governor said that in some cases the toys had few or no parental controls, and the safety limits weakened the longer the conversation continued.
“Additionally, some toys could record a child’s voice or scan their face,” the statement said.
State senator Andrew Gounardes said in a statement that “we don’t have to live in a Twilight Zone episode turned real.” LaVita Tuff with Mothers Against Media Addiction, said that “Parents should be able to feel confident that the toys their children play with are safe, which means that toys containing AI should only be sold if they are safe by design.”
Hochul has emerged as a leading elected campaigner against AI. Last month, she signed “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors” legislation prohibiting companies from offering certain unsafe chatbot features to minors, including features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage children in sexually explicit talk.
The New York measure signed Wednesday follows a similar measure in California that placed a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacture of toys with AI companions.
Earlier this week, a consortium of more than 155 child safety advocates and technology experts sent a letter to Amazon CEO Andy Jassy and eBay CEO Jamie Iannone asking the tech giants to bar AI toys from their platforms.
“Just like we don’t release cars without seat belts and test them to make sure they are safe to be driven, we shouldn’t be releasing toys that are available to the consumer before they’ve been rigorously tested,” Rachel Franz, an advocate for limitations on tech for children and leader of a program at the non-profit advocacy group Fairplay, told NBC News.
An eBay spokesperson told the network: “We continually evaluate our policies, engage with regulators, and comply with applicable laws to help ensure our marketplace remains safe, trusted, and responsive to evolving safety standards.”
An Amazon spokesperson also gave a statement to the outlet: “We require all products sold by third-party sellers in our store to comply with applicable laws and regulations,” an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement. “Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families. As reported by Fortune, […]
stories.body:
Amazon has held talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on its online marketplace, according to a report from Fortune. The discussions, which could end Amazon’s block on Muse, reportedly center on the kinds of products the AI agent recommends and the potential impact on the ecommerce giant’s advertising revenue.
Amazon is reportedly in talks to end Muse AI shopping block
Amazon is concerned that Muse AI could have an impact on its advertising revenue, according to Fortune.
As reported by Fortune, Amazon is concerned that it could lose advertising revenue by allowing Muse on its site, since it depends on actual humans seeing ads across its online marketplace. It’s also reportedly worried about the quality of the product search results that Muse will present to users, as well as whether the AI agent will affect Amazon’s relationship with customers. Neither Amazon nor Meta immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.
Though some online retailers, such as Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, and Sephora, have opened their digital doors to AI agents like Muse, Amazon has been more hesitant. Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent from shopping on its site, and has instead focused on promoting its own Alexa for Shopping assistant, which customers can now text to shop on their behalf.

stories.title: Hyperscaler Debt Boom Seen as Risk by S. Africa Central Bank
stories.summary: Sovereign borrowing is competing with increased issuance by artificial-intelligence firms and local investors are placing a greater proportion of funds in hyperscalers’ stocks, potentially raising both yields and risks, South Africa’s central bank said.

stories.title: Aidan is one of thousands of students forced to verbally defend his honours thesis as universities take on AI
stories.summary:
Honours students are increasingly being asked to sit oral assessments – but at the University of Sydney it’s become a requirement for all

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

When Aidan Elwig Pollock signed up for an honours program at the University of Sydney, he did not expect his 20,000-word thesis to be accompanied by a spoken component.

But, as AI increasingly makes written research an unreliable form of assessment, the university has demanded all students taking the one-year program defend their arguments in conversation with professors.

Continue reading...
stories.body:
When Aidan Elwig Pollock signed up for an honours program at the University of Sydney, he did not expect his 20,000-word thesis to be accompanied by a spoken component.
But, as AI increasingly makes written research an unreliable form of assessment, the university has demanded all students taking the one-year program defend their arguments in conversation with professors.
Top Australian universities are increasingly asking honours students to sit oral assessments, with Sydney the first known to require it across honours programs.
Exams have moved from computers back to paper or interviews in the four years since the release of ChatGPT made AI plagiarism a concern. Some educators have adopted the debate-focused tutorials traditional at Oxbridge colleges or the viva voce assessments typical of PhDs.
But honours programs – a year of intensive research for dedicated students after their bachelor’s degree – have been slower to adapt as they’re typically focused on a single project, which accounts for most of their grade.
Elwig Pollock, a history student, said he had not used AI at all on his work on how the commemoration of Captain Cook has evolved over time, and that the new demand was “insulting” to students and the professors who supervise them.
“If you’ve used AI to do your honours thesis and your supervisor has not figured it out throughout your regular meetings, then what’s stopping you from communicating that material successfully in a 15-minute conversation,” Elwig Pollock said.
Since 2024, Sydney bachelor’s degrees have included a mix of assessments that are vulnerable or secure to AI tools. This year, the university has formally extended that to honours programs, though the format is different for every faculty.
On Wednesday, Elwig Pollock had a short conversation which was a pass or fail hurdle task but was worth nothing towards his final grade. In his case most of his marks are coming from his thesis but his degree will not be awarded if he fails the conversation.
Engineering student Isabelle* had an entirely different experience.
Last week, the University of Sydney student had an hour of interviews with professors in a single room with five classmates, as the school rushed through assessing 250 students in two days. It accounted for 50% of her grade.
Her 20,000-word thesis was worth just 20%.
“There were people coming in and out of the room while we were being assessed so it was distracting,” said Isabelle, who asked for a pseudonym to avoid being penalised.
“[We had to] move to the other side of the room so my marker could hear me.”
The change has stressed students who aren’t used to speaking up in class, don’t speak English as a first language or need their honours to become qualified in their field – including engineers like Isabelle.
“I think it’s particularly bad in engineering because writing skills are poor, but I think it’s a Band-Aid solution,” she said of the verbal component.
Adam Bridgeman, the university’s acting deputy vice-chancellor for education, said honours degrees needed to change.
“We necessarily treat honours theses as open assessments as we can’t reliably restrict AI use,” Bridgeman said.
Staff and students were offered guidance and practice to manage the transformation and ensure English fluency and speaking ability were not “inadvertently rewarded”, he said.
“We appreciate some students might be nervous about the experience, especially if it’s their first time,” Bridgeman said. “We’ll take feedback on board as we plan for 2027 assessments.”
While Sydney is the only major institution to mandate interviews for honours programs, schools at the University of Melbourne, Monash University and Australian Catholic University are bringing them in.
Adelaide University, which was previously among the first in Australia to reintroduce viva voce tasks, is using “interactive oral assessments” in which students and teachers role-play real-world professional situations.
There are no public reports of Australia

stories.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
stories.summary: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
stories.body:
GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
- Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
- An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.
- In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.
- The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.
In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.
Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.
Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.
Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.
Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.
We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding.
